steps.user_message: I want to file my 2023 taxes correctly. I'm head of household in Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Metro Consulting: $64,800. Additional income: $11,200 (graphic design, 2 clients), $1,450 from Discover Bank savings, $320 from Fidelity. Home office: 140 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,050/month for 850 sq ft. Deductions: $2,700 student loan interest (FedLoan, 2018–2019); $720 to Habitat for Humanity have the receipt; $950 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Below I’ll walk through what looks deductible for 2023 given the items you listed, whether you should likely itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, which IRS forms you’ll need, and a few action items / questions so you can finish the return accurately.

Short summary (quick answers)
- Filing status: Head of household — OK.
- Likely best choice: Take the standard deduction ($20,800 for HOH in 2023) unless you have substantial additional itemizable amounts (state/local tax, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, or more charitable gifts).
- Student loan interest: You likely can deduct up to $2,500 (you reported $2,700 paid).
- Self-employment: Your $11,200 graphic-design income is reported on Schedule C; you’ll owe self-employment (SE) tax and can deduct half of SE tax.
- Home office: You qualify (exclusive use, 140 sq ft). You can use either the simplified method ($5/sq ft → $700) or the regular method (business % of allowable home expenses). Regular method based on your rent looks larger, but it’s limited by your net business profit.
- Interest income: Total taxable interest = $1,770 (Discover + Fidelity). Because it’s over $1,500, you must file Schedule B.
- Forms you’ll likely need: Form 1040, Schedule C, Schedule SE, Schedule 1, Schedule B, Form 8995 (if claiming QBI), and Schedule A only if you itemize. Plus Form 1098‑E for student loan interest and 1099‑NEC/1099‑INT as applicable.

Detailed walk-through and calculations

1) Total income (approximate)
- W-2 wages (Metro Consulting): $64,800
- Self-employment (graphic design): $11,200 (report on Schedule C)
- Taxable interest: $1,450 + $320 = $1,770 (report on Schedule B)
Approximate gross income = $77,770

2) Home office (you said 140 sq ft exclusive; home = 850 sq ft)
- Business-use percentage = 140 / 850 ≈ 16.4706%
- Annual rent = $2,050 × 12 = $24,600
- Regular method (apportion rent only — other allocable items like utilities/insurance/repairs could increase this): 16.4706% × $24,600 ≈ $4,052
- Simplified method = $5 × 140 sq ft = $700

Which method to pick?
- Regular method ($4,052) is much larger than simplified ($700), so regular seems better IF your net business profit is large enough to absorb it.
- Limitation: home-office deduction cannot create or increase a business loss for purposes of non-passive income limitation. In practice the home office deduction reduces your Schedule C net profit; if it reduces your net business profit to zero, you can only deduct up to the profit amount. (Excess may be carried forward in some cases.)
- Example (if your $950 unreimbursed expenses are business expenses): Schedule C expenses = $950 + home office $4,052 = $5,002 → net business profit ≈ $11,200 − $5,002 = $6,198. That is positive, so you can take the full $4,052 home-office deduction in that scenario.
- If the $950 are NOT business expenses (i.e., they are unreimbursed employee expenses), they’re nondeductible (TCJA), and cannot be used on Schedule C. You should confirm whether those $950 were costs you incurred as a self-employed designer (able to deduct) or were expenses as an employee (not deductible).

3) Self-employment tax and “above-the-line” adjustment
- If net Schedule C profit ≈ $6,198 (example above), net earnings subject to SE tax = 92.35% × $6,198 ≈ $5,725.
- SE tax ≈ 15.3% × $5,725 ≈ $876; half of that (~$438) is an adjustment to income (reduces AGI).
- You report SE tax on Schedule SE; half SE tax is reported on Schedule 1 as an adjustment.

4) Student loan interest ($2,700 paid)
- Maximum deduction = $2,500 for 2023 (you would use the $2,500 cap).
- Phaseout: for single/head-of-household in 2023, the phaseout begins at MAGI $75,000 and ends at $90,000. Whether you get the full $2,500 depends on your MAGI before this deduction.
- Using the example calculation above (after taking business deductions and half SE tax adjustment) your AGI would likely be under $75,000, so you would likely be eligible for the full $2,500 deduction. If you want, I can run a more exact approximate AGI if you confirm whether the $950 is a business expense and whether you have other deductions or income.

5) Charitable contribution ($720)
- Charitable cash donations are deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). Since the standard deduction for HOH is $20,800, and your known itemizable amounts (charity $720 + any state income tax or property tax paid) are probably well under that, you will most likely take the standard deduction.
- If you have additional itemizable items (large state income tax withheld, mortgage interest, property tax, other charitable gifts), add them up and compare to $20,800.

6) Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- You may be eligible for a 20% QBI deduction (Section 199A) on up to 20% of your qualified business income from the Schedule C. With a net profit around $6k–7k that suggests a QBI deduction in the ballpark of $1,200–$1,400 (subject to rules). If your taxable income is below the threshold for W-2 wage/QBI phase-ins ($182,100 for a head of household in 2023), the QBI deduction is generally straightforward. You’d use Form 8995 (or 8995‑A if more complex).

7) Interest reporting
- Because your taxable interest total ($1,770) exceeds $1,500, attach Schedule B to Form 1040 and list the payers (Discover, Fidelity). Also make sure you have any 1099‑INT forms.

8) Forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — business income flows from Schedule C to Schedule 1, and adjustments (half SE tax, student loan interest) appear here.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report the $11,200 and business expenses (including home office).
- Schedule SE — compute self-employment tax.
- Schedule B — for interest over $1,500.
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) — for QBI deduction if you claim it.
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (unlikely from the items you listed).
- Keep Form 1098‑E (student loan interest) and 1099‑INT and any 1099‑NEC you received.

9) Action items / questions for you (so I can refine the numbers)
- Are the $950 “unreimbursed expenses” costs of your graphic design business (supplies, software, travel, etc.)? If yes, they belong on Schedule C; if not (they were employee expenses), they are not deductible.
- Do you have 1099‑NEC forms from the two clients (or other records showing the $11,200)? Make sure to report the full amount whether or not you received 1099s.
- Do you have other deductible items not listed (mortgage interest, property taxes, large state income tax payments, additional charitable donations)?
- Do you pay for any self-employed health insurance, retirement plan contributions (SEP IRA, etc.)? Those can change AGI and tax calculations.
- Do you want me to run an approximate tax calculation (AGI, taxable income, SE tax, estimated federal tax) using the assumptions above?

10) A few practical tips
- Keep receipts and documentation for the home office (floor plan/measurement, rent, utilities, insurance, repairs) in case of questions.
- Get Form 1098‑E from your loan servicer (FedLoan) showing interest paid; also keep the receipt for Habitat donation.
- If you prepare your own return with software, the software will ask whether you want to use the simplified or regular home office method and will compute SE tax, half-SE deduction, QBI, and student loan phaseout.
- Consider meeting with a CPA or EA if you want exact tax minimization and to confirm how the home office affects other items — the rules can be nuanced and a preparer can ensure you don’t accidentally create disallowed losses.

If you want, I can:
- Run an approximate AGI and tax estimate using the two scenarios (a) $950 treated as business expenses and regular home office, and (b) $950 not deductible and home-office regular — and show the resulting student loan interest eligibility and estimated SE tax; or
- Draft a checklist email you can send to a tax preparer with all the documents they’ll need.

Which would you like next?
